content: Umbilical arterial catheters (UACs) are widely used in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs) for monitoring critically ill newborns. However, there is considerable variability in how these catheters are utilized across different NICUs. This variability includes differences in the dosing of heparin, the materials and design of the catheters, and their positioning within the body. The primary objective of this study was to evaluate whether the material used to construct umbilical arterial catheters has an impact on the incidence of ischemic events, aortic thrombosis, mortality, or necrotizing enterocolitis in neonates. To address this question, randomized and quasi-randomized controlled trials involving umbilical catheterization in newborns were reviewed. The search for relevant studies was conducted using the Cochrane Neonatal Review Group's methods, and databases such as The Cochrane Library, MEDLINE (via PubMed), CINAHL, and EMBASE were searched for studies published between 1999 and 2009. The inclusion criteria for the review were randomized studies involving newborns of any birthweight or gestational age. The studies needed to compare different catheter materials and assess clinically significant outcomes, such as ischemic events, aortic thrombosis, or catheter occlusion. Two studies were identified: one randomized and one non-randomized. The results showed no significant differences in outcomes when a heparin-bonded polyurethane catheter was used instead of a standard polyvinyl chloride (PVC) catheter. However, the non-randomized study suggested a potential benefit of using Silastic catheters, as they appeared to reduce the incidence of aortic thrombosis. The authors concluded that there is no clear evidence of clinically meaningful differences in outcomes between PVC catheters and those made from other materials. As a result, factors such as cost and availability may play a more significant role in determining which catheter material is chosen. The authors also recommended conducting a well-powered randomized trial to compare Silastic catheters with PVC catheters to provide more definitive evidence.
